name: Напад на зв’язану фігуру (1)
description:
You know that the pin is a very strong weapon. A pin is an attack on a piece that cannot or is not advised to escape. Otherwise, a stronger piece behind it falls.

Yet a pin alone is not always sufficient to win material. In fact, a pinned piece may be adequately defended. In that case, it may be beneficial to attack the pinned piece one more time.

Let's look at example 1 and example 2. In the first example, the piece behind the pinned piece is a king. In the second example, the piece standing behind the pinned piece is a piece that is worth more than the pinned piece.

What do you have to do?

Attack an opponent's pinned piece and win material.

examples.text: The black rook is pinned. It must not leave, or else the king will be in check. This is good news for white. By attacking the rook one more time with 1.g4! black has a big problem. Moving the rook is not legal and protecting the rook does not help either. White captures the rook on the next move and wins material. A pin in which the back piece is the king is often called an 'absolute pin'.

In this example, the black bishop on c2 is pinned. The difference with the previous example is that the pinned piece is allowed to move. Still, moving the piece is not wise as white can capture the rook on c8 in that case.

White takes full advantage of the pin by attacking the bishop with 1.Ne1!

A pin in which the back piece is not the king is called a 'relative pin'.
